a surname transferred from the place name, of Norwegian habitational origin, from a farm or locality named Rodal

1004582.etyen:
As a surname, a habitational name from a Norwegian farm or locality named Rodal. The medieval farm name in Halsa reflects Old Norse Róðudalr, formed from róða (“bar, pole”) + dalr (“valley”). The first element probably referred to a long ridge near the farm; an older interpretation instead treated it as a river name.
First attested in 1332 as i Roðudal.

en.g: a pizza typically eaten on Friday evening, especially as a regular family or social meal
x: I dag får vi besøk av mine foreldre, men det er Ingunns fredagspizza som vanlig.
Today my parents are visiting, but it is Ingunn's Friday pizza as usual.
kjøtt på grillen, fredagspizza, jordbær og et ubortryddet strykejern viser en jordnær og avslappet statsministerkandidat
meat on the grill, Friday pizza, strawberries and an ironing board that has not been put away present a down-to-earth and relaxed candidate for prime minister

1004838.etyen:
From fredag (“Friday”) + pizza (“pizza”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “Friday pizza”, referring to pizza eaten as a regular Friday-evening meal. The first element, Fredag, is inherited from Old Norse frjádagr (“Friday”), itself borrowed from West Germanic. The second element, pizza, is borrowed from Italian pizza. The compound is first attested in 2007.
The generic term predates the product name Grandiosa Fredagspizza, introduced in 2021.
Compare equivalent formations in Danish fredagspizza and Swedish fredagspizza (“Friday pizza”).

en.g: Gospel reading; a text or passage from one of the Gospels, especially one read during a church service
x: The parish priest read the day's Gospel reading.
Dagens evangelietekst (Matt 9,36–10,8) kommer med en stor gave til oss, for den lar alle som lytter delta i Jesu blikk.
Today's Gospel reading (Matt. 9:36–10:8) brings us a great gift, because it allows everyone listening to share in Jesus' gaze.

1005094.etyen:
Compound of evangelium (“gospel”) + tekst (“text”), with the first element appearing in the compound form evangelie- (“gospel”), literally “gospel text”.
The first element, evangelium (“gospel”), is from Latin evangelium (“gospel”), from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, gospel”). Its εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) element continues Proto-Hellenic *ehu- (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁su- (“good”); the deeper origin of the ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”) element is uncertain.
The second element, tekst (“text”), is from Old Norse textr (“text”) or texti (“text”), from Latin textus
